flashcards.q: What separates code that "works" from production-ready code?
flashcards.a: Production-ready code also handles the bad-day paths: wrong input, slow or dead services, double requests. And when something fails, the logs show it.
flashcards.more: On a laptop we only run the happy path: valid input, a good network, one user. In production all the other paths happen too, every day. So before saying "done", ask the seven questions: input, failure, repeat, permission, visibility, way back, proof.

flashcards.q: When you make an HTTP call to an outside service, what must you never leave out?
flashcards.a: A timeout. Without one, a single slow service can hold all your workers and take the whole site down.
flashcards.more: In PHP, if you say nothing, a call can wait up to 60 seconds. For that long the worker can't take any other request. A few dozen requests hanging like this use up all the workers, and even unrelated pages on the site stop. More: [[resilience/containing-failure/one-slow-call-stops-all|Containing failure]].

flashcards.q: What is the difference between timeout and max_duration in Symfony HttpClient?
flashcards.a: timeout = how long you can go without receiving any data. max_duration = the maximum time for the whole request and response together.
flashcards.more: With only a timeout, a server can trickle out a drop of data every 2 seconds and hold you for minutes, because it is never fully silent. max_duration closes that gap. On important calls, set both.

flashcards.q: After a timeout, can you assume the work didn't happen?
flashcards.a: No. A timeout means "I don't know": the work may have been done on the other side. So retry with the same idempotency key.
flashcards.more: Your request may have arrived and the work may be done, with only the response late on its way back. If you resend with a new key, the same job happens twice: two parcels, two charges. With the same key, the other side recognizes it as a repeat of the old request.

flashcards.q: What does Symfony's #[MapRequestPayload] do for you?
flashcards.a: It turns the request's JSON into a typed DTO and runs the Validator; on invalid input it returns a 422 by itself.
flashcards.more: Calling `json_decode()` by hand means checking every field and every type yourself, and forgetting one gives a 500 error. If you write `#[Assert\...]` on the DTO's properties, the rules live in one place, and only valid data reaches the controller.

flashcards.q: In what order should you look at things in a code review?
flashcards.a: Purpose, then design, then correctness and failure paths, then security and data, then tests and logs, and names and style last.
flashcards.more: The order runs from costly mistakes to cheap ones. A wrong design or a missing permission check does real damage in production and is hard to change later. Names and style can be fixed in five minutes any day, and a linter catches most of them anyway.

flashcards.q: How big can a pull request get before review quality drops?
flashcards.a: Roughly beyond 200-400 lines. Split big work into small, independent PRs.
flashcards.more: On a big PR the reviewer gets tired, skims and approves, so the real mistakes slip through. Small PRs get reviewed fast and merged fast, and when something goes wrong it is easy to find which change caused it.

flashcards.q: What is the main difference between the PHP-FPM and Node.js process models?
flashcards.a: PHP starts fresh on every request and wipes everything at the end. In Node one process runs continuously and one event loop handles all requests.
flashcards.more: That's why in PHP, whatever you put in a static variable isn't there for the next request, and even a memory leak is wiped when the request ends. With the same habit in Node, data can pass from one user to another, and memory keeps growing day after day.

flashcards.q: What is the biggest gain from learning a second ecosystem?
flashcards.a: You can tell which ideas are universal principles (timeouts, idempotency, validation) and which are just one framework's conventions.
flashcards.more: Know only one framework and every habit of it feels like "the way it must be done". Seeing a different solution to the same problem in a second one shows what the real principle was. Then you can also review other teams' code, and argue about tool choices from experience.

flashcards.q: Does fetch() in Node throw an error when the server answers 500 or 404?
flashcards.a: No. fetch only rejects on network failure or a timeout. A 500 or 404 still resolves, so you must check `response.ok` yourself.
flashcards.more: PHP's `toArray()` throws on a bad status, so PHP developers are used to errors arriving as exceptions. In Node, skip the `response.ok` check and you will parse an error page as if it were a booking. Then wrap the whole call in one try/catch that logs with context and throws your own error.

flashcards.q: What should you do before optimizing?
flashcards.a: Measure. Use a profiler to see where the time goes, then change the biggest slice.
flashcards.more: Guesses are often wrong: Ryan's team blamed the serializer while 84% of the time went into one query. Measuring finds it in 5 minutes.

flashcards.q: What is the optimization loop?
flashcards.a: Measure a baseline, find the bottleneck, change one thing, measure again. If it didn't help, revert the change.
flashcards.more: You change one thing at a time so you know which one worked. If the number doesn't move, the change is useless and doesn't need to stay in the code.

flashcards.q: Where do you look for slowness in the Symfony Profiler?
flashcards.a: In the Doctrine tab, for each query's time and for duplicates (N+1), and in the Performance tab for the timeline. It opens at `/_profiler`.
flashcards.more: `composer require --dev symfony/profiler-pack` gives you the debug toolbar. A profile is saved for every request, so you can open it later.

flashcards.q: What is Symfony Stopwatch for?
flashcards.a: Timing a specific piece of your own code. With `start()` and `stop()` it appears as a block in the Profiler timeline.
flashcards.more: At a suspicious spot, begin with `$stopwatch->start('export.load', 'app')` and end with `stop()`. Stopwatch exists in debug only, so injecting it as nullable is safe.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE?
flashcards.a: EXPLAIN only shows the plan (an estimate). EXPLAIN ANALYZE really runs the query and shows actual time and rows.
flashcards.more: ANALYZE really executes, so wrap an UPDATE or DELETE in a transaction and ROLLBACK. `Seq Scan` in the plan means reading the whole table; on a big table it usually signals a missing index.

flashcards.q: What is a spike?
flashcards.a: Time-boxed, throwaway experimental code that answers one question. The result is what you learn, not the code.
flashcards.more: "Will importing 1 million rows take 5 minutes?" is a clear question. Give it 1-2 days, write down the numbers, throw the code away. Then write the real thing cleanly.

flashcards.q: What can happen if a team skips the spike and builds a big feature on a guess?
flashcards.a: The wrong answer shows up only at launch, after weeks of work and a promise. One day of spike would have shown it on day one.
flashcards.more: Example: building a 1-million-row import with one `persist()` per row and never trying it at full size. At launch the process runs out of memory around row 200,000. A one-day spike would have shown that, and the fix, batches plus `clear()`.

flashcards.q: What harm does it do if spike code reaches production?
flashcards.a: Untested, rushed code becomes debt that haunts you for years. So throwing the code away after a spike is the rule.
flashcards.more: It starts with "let me just clean it up a bit", and two years later everyone is afraid to touch the file. Keep the numbers you learned in a note, and implement it properly.

flashcards.q: Why look at p95/p99 and not only the average?
flashcards.a: The average hides the slowest 1-5% of requests. p95/p99 show what the worst-off users experience.
flashcards.more: The average can be 120ms while p99 is 5 seconds, and users remember and complain about that slow experience. SLOs are usually written in terms of p95/p99.

flashcards.q: Where do you start reading an unfamiliar codebase?
flashcards.a: At an entry point: a route, console command, message handler, listener or scheduler. Not at the alphabetical list of files.
flashcards.more: The path of the work and the order of the files are different. Follow one request from one entry point to the end and the files you need come out by themselves.

flashcards.q: What are the entry points in a Symfony app?
flashcards.a: HTTP routes (`#[Route]`), console commands (`#[AsCommand]`), message handlers (`#[AsMessageHandler]`), event listeners and the scheduler.
flashcards.more: All of them use PHP attributes, so you can search with `grep -R "AsMessageHandler" src/`. But the debug commands hand you the list directly.

flashcards.q: How do you find out which controller a URL runs?
flashcards.a: `php bin/console debug:router --show-controllers`. For one route, `debug:router <name>` gives the details.
flashcards.more: Filter with `grep` (`| grep -i refund`) to get only the relevant routes. Next to each you see the path, the method and the controller class.

flashcards.q: What does `debug:container` tell you about a service?
flashcards.a: The service's class, its dependencies (arguments), tags and aliases. `debug:autowiring` tells you which types can be injected.
flashcards.more: Run `php bin/console debug:container 'App\Service\RefundService'` to see its configuration. A command like `debug:autowiring Mailer` tells you which interface will be autowired.

flashcards.q: How do you see which listeners run on an event?
flashcards.a: `php bin/console debug:event-dispatcher <event-name>`. You get the listeners in priority order.
flashcards.more: A question like "who sends the email when a refund happens?" is usually answered right here. To find a message handler, use `debug:messenger`.

flashcards.q: What do you gain from reading the tests?
flashcards.a: A list of the behavior the code is meant to have. `phpunit --testdox` shows it in plain language.
flashcards.more: Tests are living documents: comments go stale, but a test that keeps running tells the truth. A missing test is information too: be careful changing that part.

flashcards.q: How do you use git to find out why a line was written?
flashcards.a: Get the commit with `git blame -L start,end file`, then `git show`. To see when a word appeared, use `git log -S'word'`.
flashcards.more: The "why" lives in commit messages and PR discussions. `git log -S` (pickaxe) tells you which commit added or removed a word.

flashcards.q: Why is drawing the map by hand a good idea?
flashcards.a: Wherever you get stuck while drawing is a gap in your understanding. So the map is also a test of your understanding.
flashcards.more: One page with entry points, main services, data, outside dependencies and the questions you can't answer yet. The map also prepares you to ask a colleague.
